references.title: Azure Proactive Resiliency Library v2, Microsoft.DesktopVirtualization
references.notes: Reliability only. Each recommendation has a Resource Graph query under kql/ named by its ID. WARA runs these (ref:wara). Claim IDs are APRL's own public IDs.

claims.says: Create scaling plans per region (scaling plans, medium).
Create a validation host pool (host pools, medium).
Configure scheduled agent updates for host pools (host pools, medium).
Use a unique OU when deploying host pools with domain-joined session hosts (host pools, medium).
Protect stateful session hosts with Azure Site Recovery (host pools, medium).

references.title: Azure Resource Inventory (ARI)
references.license: MIT in the repo; the PowerShell Gallery listing says otherwise, so check before reuse

claims.says: Inventories a whole Azure environment into an Excel workbook and a diagram; it has no JSON output.
Its draw.io diagram functions (Modules/Public/PublicFunctions/Diagram/) make no Azure calls and draw from the Resource Graph rows they are given, with no AVD host pool placement.

references.title: Troubleshoot connection quality in Azure Virtual Desktop

claims.says: Up to 150 ms shouldn't affect work without rendering or video, 150 to 200 ms is fine for text, over 200 ms might affect user experience.
Review Azure's network latency statistics every two to three months in case the best region changes.

references.title: Deploy Azure Virtual Desktop (host pools and session hosts)

claims.says: Premium SSD is the recommended OS disk type for production session hosts.
Trusted launch is the default security type for new session hosts; confidential VMs are the other non-standard option.
Azure Virtual Desktop needs no public inbound ports on session hosts.

references.title: Ephemeral OS disks on Azure Virtual Desktop

claims.says: Ephemeral OS disks suit stateless hosts; the VM can't be deallocated, only restarted, reimaged or deleted.
Supported only for pooled host pools that use a session host configuration.
Not supported with an ephemeral OS disk, among others, VM deallocation, image capture, disk snapshots, Azure Disk Encryption, Azure Backup and Site Recovery.
The VM size's temp disk or cache must be at least the image's OS disk size (127 GiB for the marketplace multi-session image).
With ephemeral OS disks, set every scaling plan phase's minimum active hosts to 100% so autoscale creates and deletes hosts instead of starting and deallocating them.

references.title: Storage options for FSLogix profile containers in Azure Virtual Desktop

claims.says: Azure Files is the recommended FSLogix profile store for most customers.
Standard file shares for light workloads under 200 users; premium for light over 200 users (or several standard shares), and for medium, heavy and power workloads.

references.title: Enable GPU acceleration for Azure Virtual Desktop
references.notes: On 2026-10-20 the supported-size table still listed the NVv3 and NVv4 series, which the NV family page says retired on 2026-09-30, and didn't list NVads V710 v5. Read the table together with the current VM size pages before choosing a size.

claims.says: The page names the GPU-optimized VM series supported as session hosts and, for each, whether it supports GPU rendering and which codecs it can encode in hardware.
NC, NCv2, NCv3, ND and NDv2 sizes are generally not appropriate as session hosts; they suit compute and machine learning, not the Windows user interface.
Larger GPUs give a better experience at a given user density, and fractional GPU sizes give finer control over cost and quality; the page gives no users-per-GPU number.
VM sizes with an NVIDIA GPU come with a GRID license for 25 concurrent users.
Only Azure-distributed drivers are supported; on NVIDIA sizes only the GRID driver accelerates applications and the Windows user interface.

references.title: Azure Virtual Desktop terminology (host pools)

claims.says: Pooled hosts are updated by redeploying from updated images; personal hosts are updated in place.
Under high concurrent connection load, sessions on a host can exceed the maximum session limit.

references.title: Azure Virtual Desktop Insights glossary

claims.says: Input delay bands: good under 150 ms, acceptable 150 to 500 ms, poor 500 ms to 2 s, bad over 2 s.
Time to connect splits into user route, stack connected, logon (profiles, Group Policy, shell start, FSLogix) and shell start to shell ready; no target time is given.
Insights lists the recommended performance counters and their intervals for session hosts.

references.title: Use cases for Azure Virtual Desktop Insights

claims.says: Latency should generally be below 100 ms for ideal interaction; a session becomes broadly low quality over 200 ms.
Each session host's user input delay should ideally stay below 100 ms.
Use session history and idle host counts over time to design a scaling plan, then repeat to validate it.

references.title: Configure host pool load balancing in Azure Virtual Desktop

claims.says: Breadth-first spreads new sessions across hosts to favor session performance.
Depth-first fills one host at a time to favor cost and needs a maximum session limit.
Set the maximum session limit from measured sessions per host and host performance in Insights; the page gives no number.

references.title: Prerequisites for Azure Virtual Desktop

claims.says: Round-trip time from the client's network to the host pool's Azure region should be under 150 ms; put session hosts in the region closest to users.

references.title: Azure Virtual Desktop REST API specification, stable 2025-10-10
references.notes: The property names Resource Graph returns under properties for each AVD resource type.

claims.says: A host pool has hostPoolType, loadBalancerType, maxSessionLimit, preferredAppGroupType, startVMOnConnect, validationEnvironment, agentUpdate and publicNetworkAccess, among others.
A session host has status, sessions, allowNewSession, lastHeartBeat, agentVersion, updateState and resourceId, the virtual machine it runs on.
An application group has applicationGroupType and hostPoolArmPath, which links it to its host pool.
A scaling plan lists the host pools it applies to in hostPoolReferences, with a schedule and a time zone.

references.title: Session host update for Azure Virtual Desktop

claims.says: An update replaces one host first, then the rest in batches of a size the operator sets, so the rest of the pool stays available.
Session host update replaces VMs from the host pool's session host configuration (image, size, disk type and more); local data on the old hosts is not kept.

references.title: Windows update management methodologies for Azure Virtual Desktop session hosts

claims.says: The recommended update method depends on the session host OS (Enterprise, multi-session or Server), the kind of update and the servicing model (patch in place or image-based).
For multi-session hosts, monthly and feature updates are recommended through session host update or new Azure Compute Gallery image versions; Windows Update and Autopatch are not recommended.
For Windows Server session hosts, Azure Update Manager and automatic guest patching are the recommended monthly update methods.
Image-based servicing through session host update is recommended for pooled host pools; it keeps hosts consistent and eases rollback.
Hotpatch applies eligible monthly security updates without a reboot on supported editions, including multi-session.

references.title: Azure Files guidance for virtual desktop workloads

claims.says: Azure Files allows 2,000 concurrent handles per file and directory and 10,000 on a share's root; on SSD shares these are soft limits.
The page recommends file share type and count by concurrent FSLogix users (HDD under 2,000; one or two SSD shares with metadata caching to 5,000; more shares beyond).
Size for sign-in and sign-out storms separately from steady state; the worked example uses 10 IOPS per user steady and calls its values sample assumptions.

references.title: Configure Microsoft Defender Antivirus on a remote desktop or virtual desktop infrastructure environment
references.notes: The page's settings are the published baseline for tuning antivirus on multi-session and non-persistent hosts. It gives no measured overhead per user.

claims.says: The page lists recommended antivirus settings for VDI that balance protection and performance (randomized scans, headless UI, cloud protection and others).
Run the Defender cache maintenance task on the image before sealing it, or each VM can see higher CPU while it runs.
Security intelligence updates can come from a dedicated VDI file share instead of each VM downloading them.

references.title: Onboard non-persistent VDI devices to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint

claims.says: Choose a single entry or multiple entries per device before configuring the image.
Don't onboard the primary image or template VMs; a cloned onboarded image duplicates the sensor identity.
A VDI device's first onboarding can delay client reporting by about three to four hours.

references.title: Overview of managed disk encryption options

claims.says: Server-side encryption encrypts managed disks at rest by default, but not temp disks or disk caches.
Encryption at host adds temp disks, caches and the data flow to storage, without using the VM's CPU.
Azure Disk Encryption retires on 2028-09-15; new VMs should use encryption at host, and ADE VMs must migrate before then.
Customer-managed keys are available through a disk encryption set for server-side encryption and encryption at host.

references.title: FSLogix prerequisites

claims.says: Configure antivirus and security tools to exclude the FSLogix container files and paths the page lists.
Network latency, bandwidth and proximity to the storage provider are pivotal to the user's experience.

references.title: FSLogix container storage options

claims.says: An example FSLogix profile needs about 10 IOPS per user in steady state and 50 at sign-in and sign-out.
Proximity (latency) to the hosts and performance against the user workload are the most important factors in choosing container storage.

references.title: Troubleshoot issues using Performance Monitor (Windows Server)

claims.says: Processor time bands: up to 50% healthy, 50 to 80% worth watching, over 80% critical.
A processor queue of two or more per processor while CPU is high means looking for the processes using it.
Log counters over one or two working days, then look for patterns by day and hour rather than reacting to one reading.

references.title: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) bandwidth requirements

claims.says: The best way to know bandwidth needs is to monitor real user connections.
The page gives per-user bandwidth estimates by activity for one 1080p monitor, from idle to full-screen video.

references.title: RDP Shortpath for Azure Virtual Desktop

claims.says: RDP Shortpath sets up a UDP transport between client and host, with more reliable connections and more consistent latency; TCP reverse connect stays the fallback.

references.title: Azure Resource Graph table and resource type reference
references.notes: The source repo for this page is private, so the pin is the page's own commit and update date.

claims.says: The DesktopVirtualizationResources table holds session hosts only.
Host pools, application groups, workspaces and scaling plans are in the Resources table, with virtual machines, storage accounts, virtual networks, route tables and private endpoints.
Policy assignments are in the PolicyResources table.

references.title: Azure review checklists, Azure Virtual Desktop
references.notes: 130 items with short ID, category, WAF pillar, severity and Learn link. The AVD items have no Resource Graph query, so mapping evidence to them is ours (gap:checklist-mapping). Cite items by short ID, never by GUID.

claims.says: Prepare a local disaster recovery strategy for personal host pool session hosts (Reliability, medium).
Use zone-redundant storage for Azure Files to maximize resiliency (Reliability, high).
Session host VMs in pooled host pools shouldn't have more than 32 cores (Performance, medium).
Don't offer both full desktops and RemoteApps to the same users from the same host pool (Security, high).
Consider Start VM on Connect for personal host pools (Cost, low).
Configure scheduled agent updates (Reliability, low).
Create a validation (canary) host pool (Operations, medium).
Turn session host VMs on at least every 90 days so their tokens refresh (Operations, medium).
Enable monitoring for Azure Virtual Desktop (Reliability, high).
Send diagnostic settings for workspaces, host pools, application groups and host VMs to a Log Analytics workspace (Reliability, medium).
Evaluate a private endpoint for the Azure Files share (Security, medium).
Evaluate RDP Shortpath for clients on managed internal networks (Performance, medium).
Keep the FSLogix profile storage in the same Azure region as the session hosts (Performance, high).
Review and confirm the configured maximum FSLogix profile size (Cost, high).
Plan the best resiliency option for the host pool deployment (Reliability, high).
Build a backup protection strategy for profile and Office containers (Reliability, medium).
Determine which OS images to use for host pool deployment (Reliability, medium).
Include the latest FSLogix version in the golden image update process (Reliability, high).
Evaluate the desktop optimization tool for the image (Performance, low).
Determine whether Microsoft Teams will be part of the deployment (Performance, low).
Evaluate Gen2 VMs for host pool deployment (Performance, medium).
Consider multimedia redirection for better browser video performance (Performance, low).
For pooled host pools, select the best load balancing method (Performance, low).
Run a workload performance test to determine the best VM SKU and size (Performance, high).
Determine whether session hosts need a GPU (Performance, low).
Use VM SKUs that support Accelerated Networking (Performance, low).
Check quotas and availability for the VM sizes and types in the chosen regions (Reliability, low).
Evaluate Intune for session host management (Operations, medium).
Plan an emergency patching and update strategy for session hosts (Operations, medium).
Alert on profile storage high usage and throttling (Reliability, medium).
Check the network bandwidth needed per user and in total for the VM SKU (Performance, low).
Enable SMB multichannel on premium file shares that hold FSLogix profiles (Performance, low).
Determine which managed disk type session hosts will use (Performance, medium).
Determine the storage backend for FSLogix profiles (Performance, high).
Verify storage scalability limits against host pool requirements (Reliability, high).
With FSLogix Cloud Cache, consider putting the cache on the VM's temporary drive (Performance, low).

references.title: Session host virtual machine sizing guidelines

claims.says: The page's numbers are generic guidelines for initial performance estimates only.
Multi-session maximum users per vCPU: light 6, medium 4, heavy 2, power 1.
Keep multi-session VMs between 6 and 24 vCPUs; four cores is the lowest for a stable multi-session VM.
Plan at least 30 GB of profile storage per user.
Size capacity by a pilot (load one host while watching CPU, paging, disk and network) or by simulation tools that ramp scripted users until performance degrades.
Plan for concurrent sign-ins at the start of a shift, which are CPU-heavy, and leave headroom beyond steady state.
When memory limits density, adding memory at small sizes helps most; 8 to 16 GB can more than double the users a host supports.
Single-session minimums: light 2 vCPU and 8 GB, medium 4 vCPU and 16 GB, heavy 8 vCPU and 32 GB, each with 32 GB OS storage.
Multi-session minimums: 8 vCPU, 16 GB RAM and 32 GB OS storage for light to heavy; 6 vCPU, 56 GB and 340 GB for power.
Use GPU session hosts for graphics-heavy apps or high resolutions; CPU-only hosts encode in software and can show artifacts above 3840 x 2160 total resolution.
Use high-performance storage such as SSD or NVMe for session hosts.
Many smaller VMs beat a few large ones; they're easier to drain, update and shut down.

references.title: Use Microsoft Teams on Azure Virtual Desktop

claims.says: With media optimization, Teams calls and meetings are redirected to the local device; without it they run on the session host.
The classic Teams app for VDI reaches end of support on 2026-10-01 and end of availability on 2027-04-01.

references.title: Optimizing Windows configuration for VDI desktops

claims.says: Disk cleanup tasks should all be tested before they're used.
Removing or updating built-in Store apps can make sysprep fail; the guide links the support article.

references.title: Design review checklist for Reliability (Well-Architected Framework)
references.notes: Each pillar's checklist numbers its items (RE, SE, CO, OE, PE). The source repo is private, so the pin is the page's own git_commit_id and updated_at.

claims.says: Define reliability and recovery targets and use them as the base of the health model.
Add redundancy at several levels, especially for critical flows.
Scale on actual or predicted usage with little manual intervention.
Measure and track health continuously with uptime and reliability indicators.

references.title: Complete an Azure Well-Architected Review assessment

claims.says: The Well-Architected Review is a self-assessment of about 60 questions across the pillars, with an Azure Virtual Desktop workload variant listed under specialized reviews.
It can add Azure Advisor recommendations for one subscription or resource group only.
Brownfield workloads should repeat it on a cadence (every four months is the example), tracked as milestones.

references.title: Well-Architected Reliability Assessment (WARA)
references.notes: The owner chose WARA as the rule engine for live reliability checks (2026-10-20). Details as checked on avd-second-brain's landing-zone KB page the same day.

claims.says: Start-WARACollector, with -AVD for AVD resource types, runs APRL's queries and writes JSON.
WARA covers the Reliability pillar only.
The analyzer writes an Excel action plan; the reporter writes PowerPoint and needs Windows with PowerPoint.

references.title: Windows Desktop Optimization Tool (WDOT)
references.notes: The family's image optimization reference. Pinned to release v1.1, the commit avd-landing-zone's image build runs with a reviewed profile (scripts/image/wdot/). main (ff2574c, 2026-05-20) adds only an event log change since. WDOT supersedes VDOT, which has no license.

claims.says: Optimizations come in categories (services, scheduled tasks, autologgers, default user settings, local policy, network, disk cleanup, Appx packages and more), each item set to apply or skip in a JSON profile.
Only items whose OptimizationState is Apply run; the templates are a starting profile to review, not a verdict on every estate.
The optimizations change system behavior and should be tested outside production first.
The repository's LICENSE file is MIT, while its README and EULA describe sample code terms (illustration only, as is), and a non-interactive run must accept the EULA.

observations.observed: The landing zone turns encryption at host on by default and registers the subscription feature it needs, so it never uses Azure Disk Encryption. No run has measured whether it changes host performance, which the source says it doesn't.

The landing zone's session hosts use Premium SSD OS disks, as the source recommends for production. No run has compared disk latency on Standard SSD or an ephemeral OS disk, so the choice rests on the source, not our evidence.
Latency measured from Cloud Shell says nothing about users, because Cloud Shell runs in an Azure datacenter. Measure round-trip time from the user's device, against endpoints verified to be regional.

The landing zone's minimum kit defaults to a 4-vCPU memory-optimized host, which is Microsoft's stated floor and below its 6 to 24 vCPU range, chosen for the smallest test cost. The reasoning that shared hosts run out of memory before CPU is our hypothesis; no measurement backs it yet.

Adopted as the landing zone's automatic sizing input, and its preflight warns above 6 sessions per vCPU. No real users have been measured against it, so the numbers are still Microsoft's prior, not our evidence.
The landing zone's image build keeps WDOT's Appx package removal off for this reason; no sysprep failure has been seen with it off. Not yet tested with it on.

WDOT's DiskCleanup category deletes every log, trace and event log file on the system drive, including an image build's own evidence before the image test reads it. The landing zone keeps that category off and cleans narrowly instead.

What runs inside the guest isn't visible from the control plane, but the landing zone's image build tags each gallery image version with the WDOT release, commit and profile hash it ran, so a Reader can see which pin and profile an image claims. Images built any other way carry no such record.
